name: Aluminum chloride hexahydrate (Drysol)
lead: Aluminium chloride hexahydrate is the active ingredient in prescription-strength antiperspirants such as Drysol, used for hyperhidrosis (excessive sweating). Dermatology sources describe topical aluminium chloride as a first-line treatment, in higher concentrations than ordinary antiperspirants, which typically use aluminium chlorohydrate [1][2]. It acts as an astringent that reduces sweat output [2].

Its most common side effect is skin irritation [1]. The US product label found carries the statement that sale and use are restricted to a physician or licensed practitioner [3]. Sweating is sometimes discussed in appearance culture because of visible sweat marks and odour; formal evidence comes from hyperhidrosis research.

paras: Reference works say effects take roughly three to five days to appear and that it works especially well on the underarms [1]. Treatment guidelines cited recommend topical antiperspirants first, ahead of oral drugs, injections or devices [1].

Irritation is the commonly reported effect [1]. The hexahydrate is an acidic salt and the anhydrous form is corrosive in industrial handling [2]. A 2005 review examined aluminium in antiperspirants in relation to breast cancer [4]; animal studies have explored aluminium chloride toxicity in other contexts [5].

A registered trial compared non-prescription with prescription topical treatments and no treatment for sweating (24 participants) [6]. Other registered studies compared topical aluminium chloride with botulinum toxin injections in residual-limb hyperhidrosis [7] and tested antiperspirant in prosthesis users [8].

card.summary: Prescription-strength antiperspirant salt; guideline first-line for hyperhidrosis, with irritation the main downside.

quick.overview:
Aluminium chloride hexahydrate is the active ingredient in prescription antiperspirants like Drysol. Guidelines cited by dermatology references list topical antiperspirants as first-line for excessive sweating.

A few small registered studies compare it with other treatments.
quick.mechanism: It is an astringent salt that reduces sweat output at the skin. Improvement is described as taking several days.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is the common effect. The label restricts sale to licensed practitioners. Aluminium exposure has been studied in other contexts, including a 2005 review on antiperspirants and breast cancer.
